title: How to Restore Gun Rights After a Felony Conviction
description: How firearm rights can be restored after a conviction: the federal rules, the application process reopened in 2026, and how ten states handle it.
intro: Federal law bars people with certain convictions from having firearms or ammunition. Those rights can be restored in some cases, through state relief, a federal application, or both. Which route applies depends on where the conviction happened and what kind it was.

The federal application route was unusable from 1992 until recently. The Department of Justice reopened it in 2026 under a new process called Federal Firearm Rights Restoration. Approval is not automatic.
State and federal rules work separately. Relief under one does not always remove the ban under the other. This page is general information, not legal advice.

sections.heading: Who the federal gun ban covers
paragraphs: The main federal rule is 18 U.S.C. 922(g). It lists nine groups of people who may not possess, ship, transport or receive firearms or ammunition. Two of the groups are based on convictions:
bullets: Anyone convicted in any court of a crime punishable by imprisonment for more than one year. The test is the sentence the crime could carry, not the time actually served.

Anyone convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. This is a misdemeanor involving the use or attempted use of physical force, or the threatened use of a deadly weapon, committed by someone in a listed relationship to the victim, such as a current or former spouse, a parent or guardian, a person who shares a child with the victim, or a current or recent former dating partner.

sections.heading: When a conviction stops counting under federal law
paragraphs: Federal law says a conviction that has been expunged (cleared from the record), set aside (canceled by a court) or pardoned (officially forgiven), or for which the person has had civil rights restored, is not treated as a conviction. There is one exception. It still counts if the pardon, expungement or restoration expressly says the person may not ship, transport, possess or receive firearms.

The wording of the relief matters. In Caron v. United States (1998), the Supreme Court held that where a state restored a person's rights but still restricted handguns, the convictions still counted for the federal ban on all firearms.

The relief must also come from the jurisdiction that entered the conviction. In Beecham v. United States (1994), the Court held that a state restoration of civil rights did not remove the federal ban for a federal conviction.

A separate 5-year rule covers a single misdemeanor domestic violence conviction based on a dating relationship, with conditions. The 2022 changes on dating relationships do not apply to convictions entered before June 25, 2022.

sections.heading: The federal application process reopened in 2026
paragraphs: Under 18 U.S.C. 925(c), a barred person may apply to the Attorney General for relief from the federal ban. The Attorney General may grant it if satisfied that the applicant will not be likely to act in a manner dangerous to public safety and that relief would not be contrary to the public interest.

From 1992, Congress barred the use of federal funds to process these applications. A final rule published on August 20, 2026 and effective September 21, 2026 set up a new process. Applications opened to invited candidates on September 25, 2026 and to the public on November 4, 2026, when the Department said the first 5,000 candidates can apply. The next date listed is January 4, 2027, when 500 more candidates can apply and the application fee will begin.
It could not be confirmed whether the 5,000 cap has been reached, what the 500 figure means in practice, or how long decisions take. The steps the Department lists are:
bullets: An online application. Once started, it must be completed within 30 days.
A $30 non-refundable fee. Applicants may ask for it to be waived or reduced and must give the reason. The criteria for waivers had not been published.
Electronic fingerprints, taken at a participating US Post Office after the first part of the application is submitted and a QR code arrives by email.
Character references, then contact with restoration specialists and a final decision.

sections.heading: Applications the 2026 rule says will be denied
paragraphs: The rule lists situations in which an application will be denied, absent extraordinary circumstances. This is a partial summary. The full list is in the rule.
bullets: With no time limit: felony convictions involving, among others, the death of another person, sexual assault, kidnapping, domestic violence, burglary, robbery, arson, assault, stalking, or brandishing or discharging a firearm.

Within the last 10 years, counting the conviction or any part of the sentence: felonies involving, among others, drug manufacture or distribution, threats of violence or explosives, and a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence.
Within the last 5 years: any other felony, and any assault, battery or stalking offense or threatened act of violence.
Current status: for example, awaiting sentence, serving any part of a sentence, or taking part in a diversion program.

sections.heading: What a federal grant does and does not do
paragraphs: A grant removes the federal ban for which relief was sought. The FBI then updates the national background check system (NICS). A person who later becomes subject to a new ban must reapply.

A grant does not remove a separate ban under state law. After a denial, the person may ask the US district court where they live to review the decision, and can usually reapply after a waiting period.

sections.heading: How state restoration works in ten states
paragraphs: States use different methods. Some restore rights automatically after a waiting period. Some require a petition (a written request) to a court. Some leave the decision to a pardon or parole board.

The table shows ten states with a process set out in a state source. Only these ten were checked, so nothing here describes any other state. Each state's rules have exclusions and conditions that are not listed.

headers: Main rule in the state source
rows: A judicial officer, at their discretion (A.R.S. 13-910)
Never available for a dangerous offense. For a serious offense, not until 10 years after absolute discharge.
State Board of Pardons and Paroles
Restoring civil and political rights does not include firearm rights, which the Board must grant specifically. The Board cannot restore firearm rights for a federal conviction.
Automatic for most felonies; Commission of Pardons and Parole for listed felonies (Idaho Code 18-310)
Rights return on final discharge for most felonies. For listed felonies, an application is possible no sooner than 5 years after final discharge.

The ban ends 3 years after fines are paid and imprisonment, probation and parole are completed. For a specified felony, 5 years plus restoration under MCL 28.424. For a misdemeanor involving domestic violence, 8 years.

For a person barred because of a crime of violence. The court may restore the right for good cause if the person has been released from physical confinement. After a denial, a 3-year wait unless the court allows earlier.
One nonviolent felony only. Civil rights restored for at least 20 years. One year's residence. $200 filing fee unless indigent.
Court of common pleas in the county of residence (R.C. 2923.14)
Requires completion of sentence and supervision and a law-abiding life since.
Circuit court in the county of residence (ORS 166.274)
The petitioner must show by clear and convincing evidence that they are not a threat to public safety or themselves.
Circuit court where the person lives (Va. Code 18.2-308.2(C))
A person convicted of a felony may petition only after civil rights have been restored by the Governor or other appropriate authority. The court may grant for good cause.
Superior court in the county that entered the prohibition (RCW 9.41.041)

5 crime-free years in the community for a felony and listed misdemeanors; 3 years for other non-felony crimes. Not available for felony sex offenses, class A felonies, or felonies with a maximum sentence of 20 years or more.

sections.heading: Why state restoration may not lift the federal ban
paragraphs: The Department of Justice states that state restoration of rights does not remove disabilities (legal bans) imposed by a federal conviction, and that a state restoration of a state conviction also may not remove federal disabilities. The sources give three reasons:
bullets: The conviction was federal. Only federal relief counts for it.
The state relief leaves some firearm restriction in place. That triggers the exception described above.
For a misdemeanor domestic violence conviction, restored civil rights only help if the law of that jurisdiction takes civil rights away for that offense in the first place.

lede: Maybe it's been years since your conviction and you've rebuilt a lot of your life, but this one question still hangs over you: can I legally own a gun again? Not knowing where you stand is its own kind of stress.

Here's the plain answer to start with. Federal law bars people with certain convictions from having firearms or ammunition, but those rights can be restored in some cases, through state relief, a federal application, or both. Which route applies depends on where the conviction happened and what kind it was.

The federal application route was unusable from 1992 until recently. The Department of Justice reopened it in 2026 under a new process called Federal Firearm Rights Restoration. Approval is not automatic.

This guide walks through who the federal ban covers, when a conviction stops counting, how the new federal application works, and how ten states handle restoration. State and federal rules work separately, so relief under one does not always remove the ban under the other. This page is general information, not legal advice.
takeaways: Federal law bars two groups based on convictions from having firearms or ammunition: anyone convicted of a crime punishable by more than one year in prison (whatever time was actually served), and anyone convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence.

A conviction that has been expunged, set aside or pardoned, or for which civil rights have been restored, is not treated as a conviction under federal law, unless the relief expressly says the person may not have firearms.

The Department of Justice reopened the federal application in 2026. The steps are an online application, a $30 non-refundable fee (listed to begin January 4, 2027, and you can ask for a waiver or reduction), fingerprints and character references. Approval is not automatic.
State and federal relief work separately. State restoration may not lift the federal ban, and a federal grant does not remove a separate state ban.
States use different methods: some restore rights automatically after a waiting period, some require a petition to a court, and some leave it to a pardon or parole board.

Pull out the paperwork for any pardon, expungement or restoration you already have and read its wording. Under federal law, a line that restricts firearms keeps the conviction counting.
If the federal application interests you, check the Department of Justice program page at justice.gov/ffrr for its current dates, fee and waiver details.
Ask a legal aid office or an attorney to look at your situation. /free-expungement-help lists free legal aid by state, and /cities lists attorneys by city.

title: How to Remove an Eviction From Your Record
description: How eviction records can be sealed, expunged or disputed: the federal seven-year limit, state sealing laws in 18 states and DC, and dispute steps.
intro: An eviction is a civil court case, not a criminal one, so it is cleared under different laws from a criminal record, and the criminal-record rules on the state pages of this site do not apply to it.

An eviction case can come off your record in two main ways. A state law can seal or expunge the court record, which means hiding it from the public or removing it. And federal law generally stops screening companies from reporting an eviction after seven years.

Whether sealing is available depends on the state. Laws of this kind were confirmed in 18 states and the District of Columbia, though South Carolina's does not take effect until January 1, 2027. Some laws work automatically. Others require a request to the court.
Errors on a tenant screening report are a separate problem. Federal law sets out a way to dispute them.

sections.heading: What an eviction record is and where it shows up
paragraphs: An eviction case creates court records: the complaint, proof of service, the court's orders and other papers. A filing is not the same as a judgment (the court's final decision). A case can be withdrawn, dismissed, settled or decided for the tenant and still leave a court record.

Tenant screening reports can include eviction records, criminal records, civil judgments and credit history. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) says the final outcome should be shown, for example dismissed. One eviction should not be listed several times, and sealed or expunged evictions should not appear.

sections.heading: The federal seven-year limit
paragraphs: The Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) is the federal law covering companies that sell background reports. Under it, these companies may not report civil suits and civil judgments that are more than seven years old, or until the governing statute of limitations (a legal deadline) has expired, whichever is longer. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says the limit covers most civil lawsuits and judgments, including housing court cases.

The limit does not apply to reports used for credit or life insurance of $150,000 or more, or for a job with an annual salary of $75,000 or more. It also limits only the reporting companies. It does not remove the case from the court's own records. That depends on state law.

sections.heading: State laws that seal or limit eviction records
paragraphs: The table lists every state law that could be confirmed. The list may not be complete. It is not a 50-state survey, and states not listed were not individually checked. Georgia and Texas were looked at, but their rules could not be confirmed. Laws change, and each row gives the year shown in the source.

Wisconsin has a related law that is not a sealing law. It sets minimum periods that eviction cases stay on the state's online court record site: at least 10 years where a writ of restitution (an eviction order) was granted, and at least 2 years where the case was dismissed with no money judgment.
These laws bind courts. Some also bind screening companies (Connecticut, Massachusetts, Utah and Washington). How quickly private databases are updated in practice could not be confirmed.

rows: Court seals the case when it is dismissed before judgment or decided for the tenant, or when landlord and tenant agree in writing to set aside the eviction order and seal.
Court order on dismissal or tenant win (no motion mentioned in the text); or by joint agreement

Clerk limits access to the parties and a few others. The record opens to the public only if the landlord prevails within 60 days of filing, or by court order after a later trial judgment for the landlord.
Records are suppressed (not publicly available) while the case is open. They become public if the court grants the landlord possession, unless the parties agree otherwise.
The case is removed from the court website within 30 days after withdrawal, dismissal or nonsuit, or a judgment for the tenant. Removed records cannot be used for tenant screening.
Records are sealed 30 days after the case ends if there was no judgment for possession for the landlord, and 3 years after if there was. A tenant can also ask at any time on listed grounds.

Records are shielded from the public when the whole case was dismissed, no appeal is pending, and either 3 years have passed since filing or the parties file an agreement. Applies to cases filed on or after January 1, 2025.
Automatic; a separate petition to seal is also possible

Court may seal a case that was sufficiently without a basis in fact or law where sealing is clearly in the interests of justice. It must seal certain cases linked to foreclosure and certain dismissed cases.
Part discretionary, part mandatory; the law does not say whether a motion is needed
Court must order the record sealed when the case is dismissed, and in other listed situations.
Automatic since July 1, 2025; by request before that

In failure-to-pay-rent cases, records are shielded within 60 days after the case ends if there was no judgment of possession. If there was one, the tenant can ask after redeeming and waiting 12 months, or for good cause. Does not apply to cases started before October 1, 2024.
Automatic without a judgment of possession; by motion otherwise

Tenant may petition to seal: no-fault evictions at any time after the case ends; dismissed cases or tenant wins at any time; non-payment cases after 4 years; fault cases after 7 years, with conditions.
Court must expunge when the tenant won, the case was dismissed, the parties agree, or 3 years have passed since the eviction was ordered, among other grounds.
Mostly automatic; some grounds need the tenant's motion
In summary eviction cases, the file is sealed when the case is dismissed, 10 judicial days after it is denied, or 31 days after the tenant's affidavit if the landlord does not follow up.
Automatic, plus by motion or agreement

A person evicted for non-payment or damage, who has resolved all claims, may move to seal 7 years after the eviction order was satisfied if not evicted again in that time. A separate rule covers domestic violence victims.

Tenant may move to set aside the judgment and seal: after 5 years for a judgment against the tenant if any money award is satisfied, or after a judgment or dismissal in the tenant's favor. Courts also seal eligible cases each year.
By motion, plus automatic yearly sealing
Court must seal on a party's motion where the case was dismissed, an agreement was satisfied, or any money judgment was paid in full. One request every 5 years.
Eviction filings must be removed from the public index 7 years after final disposition or filing, if no further filing has been recorded. Not yet in force.
Appears automatic (no request process in the text)

Court expunges when the whole case was dismissed, no appeal is pending and 3 years have passed since filing, or when landlord and tenant file an agreement. A tenant can also petition in non-payment and lease-expiry cases once any judgment is satisfied.

In general district court, cases dismissed (after 30 days) or nonsuited (after 6 months) with no order of possession are expunged. For a judgment for the tenant, and for cases started before July 1, 2024, the tenant petitions.
Automatic for dismissals and nonsuits; by petition otherwise

Court may issue an order for limited dissemination where the landlord's case lacked sufficient basis, the tenancy was reinstated, or for other good cause. Screening providers must then not disclose the case.
Court order (the law does not say how it is requested)

sections.heading: Setting aside a judgment or reaching an agreement
paragraphs: Courts have procedures to set aside (cancel) a judgment in limited circumstances. As one example, California's court system says a tenant can ask only for reasons such as mistake, inadvertence, surprise or excusable neglect, within 6 months of the judgment, and only once. Rules and deadlines differ in every state.

Several laws allow sealing or expungement when landlord and tenant agree: Arizona, Idaho, Minnesota, Nevada and Utah. The FTC also notes that a tenant can ask a former landlord, in writing, to send updated or correct information to the court.

sections.heading: Paying the judgment
paragraphs: Paying a money judgment does not by itself remove the record. But several state laws make it a condition of relief: Rhode Island, Oregon, Utah and North Dakota. In Utah, a Satisfaction of Judgment must be filed with the court.

In Massachusetts, the party who won a non-payment judgment must file a notice of satisfaction within 14 days of being paid. If they do not, the person who paid can ask the court to treat it as satisfied.

sections.heading: Disputing errors on a tenant screening report
paragraphs: Under the FCRA, when a consumer disputes an item, the screening company must reinvestigate free of charge. It must record the item's current status or delete it within 30 days of receiving the dispute. That can be extended by up to 15 days if the consumer sends more information during the 30 days. An item found to be inaccurate, incomplete or unverifiable must be promptly deleted or modified.
The FTC says renters can check housing court records before applying and, if the records are wrong or incomplete, can ask the court to correct them. The dispute steps the FTC and CFPB describe are:
bullets: Contacting the screening company in writing and describing each error.
Including copies of supporting documents, such as paperwork showing how the eviction case was resolved.
Contacting whoever supplied the wrong information. For eviction record errors, this can include the court.
Telling the landlord about the dispute, then giving the landlord the corrected report or asking the company to send it.

sections.heading: Getting your report and filing a complaint
paragraphs: If a landlord turns you down, asks for a co-signer or charges more because of a report, the landlord must give you the screening company's name, address and phone number. You can get a free copy from that company if you ask within 60 days.

Problems with tenant screening can be reported to the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov/complaint or (855) 411-2372, and to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Legal aid offices and attorneys handle eviction record matters. This page is general information, not legal advice.

lede: An eviction on your record can make every rental application feel like a test you've already failed. If a landlord has turned you down, or you're bracing for it, you're not alone, and the law does give you some tools.

First, an eviction is a civil court case, not a criminal one. It is cleared under different laws from a criminal record, so the criminal-record rules on the state pages of this site do not apply to it.

An eviction case can come off your record in two main ways. A state law can seal or expunge the court record, which means hiding it from the public or removing it. And federal law generally stops screening companies from reporting an eviction after seven years.

This guide covers that seven-year limit, the sealing laws confirmed in 18 states and the District of Columbia (South Carolina's does not take effect until January 1, 2027), and the federal steps for disputing errors on a tenant screening report. Some sealing laws work automatically; others require a request to the court.
takeaways: An eviction is a civil case, not a criminal one, so the criminal-record rules on this site's state pages do not apply to it.
Federal law generally stops screening companies from reporting an eviction after seven years, but that limit does not remove the case from the court's own records.
Laws that seal or limit eviction records were confirmed in 18 states and the District of Columbia. Some work automatically; others require a request to the court.
The CFPB says a screening report should show the final outcome, should not list one eviction several times, and should not include sealed or expunged evictions.
You can dispute errors with the screening company free of charge. It generally has 30 days to reinvestigate and must delete or fix items that are inaccurate, incomplete or unverifiable.

title: Expunged Record Showing on a Background Check: What to Do
description: What federal law says when an expunged or wrong record shows on a background check: dispute steps, deadlines, employer duties, damages and fees.
intro: An expunged or sealed record is not supposed to show up on a background check. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) tells consumers that expunged criminal records should not appear on a report. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) lists sealed or expunged records as a common type of error.

If one does appear, the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) lets you dispute it with the background check company at no charge. The company generally has 30 days to reinvestigate. It must delete or correct information that is inaccurate, incomplete or cannot be verified.
If a dispute does not fix the problem, complaints can be filed with the CFPB or the FTC, and the law also allows lawsuits. This page is general information, not legal advice.

sections.heading: What the law requires of background check companies
paragraphs: The FCRA is the federal law covering background check companies, which it calls consumer reporting agencies. When a company prepares a report, it must follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information about the person.

A company that reports public records likely to hurt someone's ability to get a job must do one of two things. It must tell the person, at the time, that the information is being reported and to whom. Or it must keep strict procedures so the information is complete and up to date.

The statute does not mention expunged or sealed records by name. Whether a particular report breaks the reasonable procedures rule is decided case by case. Court decisions on this point were not researched for this page. State laws, some stricter than the FCRA, were not checked either.

sections.heading: What the FTC and CFPB have said
paragraphs: FTC guidance for screening companies lists reports that include criminal records that have been expunged or otherwise sealed as a sign that a company's procedures may not be reasonable.

In October 2023, the FTC and CFPB alleged that a tenant screening company failed to put in place reasonable procedures to keep sealed eviction records out of its reports. The settlement was $15 million.

In January 2024 the CFPB issued a more detailed advisory opinion on expunged and sealed records. It withdrew that opinion on May 12, 2025, and said the withdrawal is not necessarily final. The statute itself is unchanged. No 2026 statement from either agency on this topic was found.

sections.heading: What employers must do
paragraphs: An employer may not get a report unless it has given you a separate written disclosure and you have authorized the report in writing.

Before taking adverse action (a negative decision, such as not hiring you) based on the report, the employer must give you a copy of the report and a written description of your rights. The statute sets no number of days the employer must wait.

After the decision, the employer must give notice of the action, the name, address and phone number of the company that supplied the report, and notice of your right to a free copy within 60 days and to dispute the report. Landlords must give the same notice after turning someone down because of a report.

sections.heading: The dispute steps
paragraphs: The FTC and CFPB describe these steps:
bullets: Getting the report. The employer must hand over a copy before acting on it. The background check company must also provide a free copy if asked no later than 60 days after the adverse action notice.
Reviewing it. The CFPB says to check that misdemeanors and felonies are listed accurately, that one charge does not appear several times, and that expunged or removed records do not appear.

Disputing in writing with the background check company. The CFPB says to include copies, not originals, of documents that show the accurate information, and suggests certified mail with return receipt.
Contacting the source. The CFPB says to contact whoever reported the incorrect information as well. For criminal record errors, this can include the court.
Checking the result. The FTC says to check that the errors are gone and to ask the company to send the corrected report to the employer.

sections.heading: What the company must do, and by when
paragraphs: The FCRA sets these duties and deadlines for the company:
bullets: Within 5 business days of receiving the dispute: notify whoever supplied the information and pass on the relevant information you sent.

Within 30 days of receiving the dispute: complete a reasonable reinvestigation, free of charge, and record the item's current status or delete it. This can be extended by up to 15 days if you send relevant information during the 30 days.
If the item is found to be inaccurate or incomplete, or cannot be verified: promptly delete or modify it.
Within 5 business days after finishing: send written results, including a copy of the revised report.

sections.heading: If the dispute does not fix it
paragraphs: The company may end a reinvestigation if it reasonably decides the dispute is frivolous or irrelevant, including where it was not given enough information. It must say so within 5 business days, with reasons. The CFPB notes that some states set shorter deadlines.

If the reinvestigation does not resolve the dispute, you may file a brief statement setting out the dispute. After a deletion or a dispute notation, you can ask the company to notify anyone you name who received the report in the past two years for employment purposes, or the past six months for any other purpose.
Complaints can be submitted to the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov/complaint or to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

sections.heading: What the law says about lawsuits, damages and fees
paragraphs: The FCRA allows a person to sue over violations. This is what the statute says. It is not a prediction about any case. The statute does not promise any result and does not say that a case costs nothing to bring. Legal aid offices and attorneys handle FCRA matters.
bullets: Willful violations (the statute's word for the more serious kind): the violator is liable for any actual damages, or damages of not less than $100 and not more than $1,000, plus such punitive damages (damages meant to punish) as the court may allow.
Negligent violations (failing to take proper care): the violator is liable for any actual damages. This section has no fixed minimum amount and no punitive damages.
Costs and attorney's fees: in both sections, the court awards the costs of the action and reasonable attorney's fees only in the case of a successful action, in an amount determined by the court.

Fees can also go the other way. If the court finds that an unsuccessful pleading, motion or other paper was filed in bad faith or for purposes of harassment, it must award the prevailing party attorney's fees reasonable in relation to the work of responding.
Time limit: an action must be brought not later than the earlier of 2 years after the person discovers the violation, or 5 years after the violation occurs.

lede: You did the hard part. You got your record cleared, and then it showed up anyway on a background check, maybe just as a job or an apartment was within reach. That is maddening.

It also isn't rare, and it isn't how things are supposed to work. An expunged or sealed record is not supposed to show up on a background check. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) tells consumers that expunged criminal records should not appear on a report, and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) lists sealed or expunged records as a common type of error.

The Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) lets you dispute it with the background check company at no charge. The company generally has 30 days to reinvestigate, and it must delete or correct information that is inaccurate, incomplete or cannot be verified.

This guide walks through what background check companies and employers must do, the dispute steps and deadlines, and what the law allows if a dispute does not fix the problem, including complaints and lawsuits. This page is general information, not legal advice.
takeaways: An expunged or sealed record is not supposed to show up on a background check, and the FTC lists it as a common type of error.

You can dispute it with the background check company at no charge. The company generally has 30 days to reinvestigate and must delete or correct information that is inaccurate, incomplete or cannot be verified.
Before an employer takes a negative decision based on a report, it must give you a copy of the report and a written description of your rights.
After being turned down, you can get a free copy of the report from the background check company if you ask within 60 days.

If a dispute does not fix it, you can file complaints with the CFPB or the FTC, and the law allows lawsuits, within a time limit of 2 years after discovering the violation or 5 years after it happened, whichever comes first.

headings.What employers must do: What Does an Employer Have to Do Before Turning Me Down?
headings.The dispute steps: How Do I Dispute the Report?

keys.What the law requires of background chec: When a company prepares a report, it must follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information about the person.
keys.What the FTC and CFPB have said: FTC guidance for screening companies lists reports that include criminal records that have been expunged or otherwise sealed as a sign that a company's procedures may not be reasonable.
keys.What employers must do: Before taking adverse action (a negative decision, such as not hiring you) based on the report, the employer must give you a copy of the report and a written description of your rights.
keys.The dispute steps: You can dispute in writing with the background check company, including copies, not originals, of documents that show the accurate information.
keys.What the company must do, and by when: Within 30 days of receiving the dispute, the company must complete a reasonable reinvestigation, free of charge, and record the item's current status or delete it.
keys.If the dispute does not fix it: Complaints can be submitted to the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov/complaint or to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
keys.What the law says about lawsuits, damage: An action must be brought not later than the earlier of 2 years after the person discovers the violation, or 5 years after the violation occurs.

next_steps: Get a copy of the report: from the employer before it acts, or free from the background check company if you ask within 60 days of the adverse action notice.
Check it line by line: that misdemeanors and felonies are listed accurately, that one charge does not appear several times, and that expunged records do not appear.

Dispute in writing with the background check company, with copies (not originals) of your documents. The CFPB suggests certified mail with return receipt. You can also contact the court if it supplied the wrong information.
Once the result comes back, check that the errors are gone and ask the company to send the corrected report to the employer.

If it still isn't fixed, you can complain to the CFPB or FTC and ask a legal aid office or attorney about your options. /free-expungement-help lists free legal aid by state, and /cities lists attorneys by city.

title: Traveling With a Criminal Record: Passports, Canada and Mexico
description: Can a felon get a passport or travel to Canada or Mexico? What the law says about passports, probation, DUIs at the Canadian border and coming home.
lede: Maybe there's a wedding in Toronto, a family trip to Cancún, or a job that needs you on the road. And somewhere in the back of your mind is the question of whether your record is going to follow you to the airport and get you turned around in front of everyone.

Here is the good news first: a criminal record on its own does not stop a US citizen from getting a passport, and it cannot keep a citizen from coming home. Most of the real roadblocks are narrower than people fear.

The places where a record does matter are specific. A few situations block a passport, probation and parole limit when you can leave, Canada is strict (especially about DUIs), and Mexico has the power to refuse entry but doesn't publish a list of crimes.
This guide walks through each of those using the actual laws and official pages, and it tells you plainly where the official sources were silent or contradicted each other.
takeaways: A criminal record by itself is not a listed reason to deny a US passport. Open felony warrants, travel bans in probation or parole conditions, certain drug-trafficking convictions, child support arrears over $2,500 and large federal tax debts can be.
On probation, supervised release or parole, you need permission to leave the country, and federal officers are told to get the court's express consent first.

Canada can refuse entry for many US convictions, and a DUI on or after December 18, 2018 counts as serious criminality there. Deemed rehabilitation, criminal rehabilitation and a Temporary Resident Permit are the ways in.
Mexico's law lets officers refuse entry when a person's record threatens national or public security, but it lists no specific crimes and refusal is discretionary.
A US citizen with a record can't be refused re-entry to the US for that record, but an open warrant can still lead to arrest at the border.

sections.heading: Can I Get a Passport With a Felony?
paragraphs: For most people, yes. No federal statute or regulation we read lists having a criminal record in general as a reason to deny a US passport. Instead, the passport rules (22 CFR 51.60) list specific situations, some where the State Department "may not issue" a passport and others where it "may refuse."

Most of those situations are about where you are right now in the system, not what you did years ago: an open felony warrant, a court order or probation condition that bars you from leaving the country, or being in prison or on parole for certain drug crimes. A finished sentence for an ordinary felony is not on the list.

The same rules work in reverse. Under 22 CFR 51.62, the State Department "may revoke or limit a passport" if the holder is someone who could be denied one. When a passport is denied or revoked, it "may issue a limited validity passport good only for direct return to the United States."

sections.heading: What Can Stop Me Getting a Passport?
paragraphs: The one conviction-based rule that is mandatory is for drug offenses involving a border. Under 22 U.S.C. 2714, a passport "may not be issued" to someone convicted of a felony drug offense, federal or state, "if the individual used a passport or otherwise crossed an international border in committing the offense." Any passport already issued to that person must be revoked. Drug misdemeanors can be covered too, but only if the Secretary of State decides to apply the rule to that person, and the law says it "does not apply to an individual's first conviction for a misdemeanor which involves only possession of a controlled substance."

This drug bar is temporary. It lasts only while the person "is imprisoned, or is legally required to be imprisoned," or "is on parole or other supervised release after having been imprisoned as the result of that conviction." "Imprisoned" includes a halfway house, a treatment facility or similar place, full or part time. Passports can still be issued "in emergency circumstances or for humanitarian reasons."

Other rules apply to people convicted of certain sex offenses. A "covered sex offender" can only get a passport book that carries a "conspicuous identifier," and cannot get a passport card. A separate mandatory bar covers people convicted under 18 U.S.C. 2423 who used a passport or crossed a border in committing the offense, during the period the law covers.

Two money problems can also block a passport, and they catch many people with records by surprise because they have nothing to do with a conviction. First, a passport may not be issued if HHS has certified that you owe child support arrears above the amount set by law. That amount is more than $2,500 (42 U.S.C. 652(k)), lowered from $5,000 in 2006.

Federal tax debt works the same way. A "seriously delinquent tax debt" is, by statute, an assessed federal tax debt "greater than $50,000," adjusted each year for inflation, with a lien or levy. The IRS lists the adjusted figure as $64,000 for 2025 and $66,000 for 2026. Debts being paid on time under an installment agreement or offer in compromise do not count.

If your application is caught by the tax rule, the IRS says the State Department holds it open for 90 days so you can pay or set up a payment plan. With an expedited request, the IRS can generally cut its 30-day decertification time to "9-16 days."

We could not read the State Department's or HHS's own pages on child support and passports (both blocked our access), so the details of how to clear a child support hold are not covered here. Your state child support agency can tell you where you stand.

sections.heading: Can I Leave the Country While on Probation or Parole?
paragraphs: Not without permission, and for international travel the bar is higher. The standard federal condition reads: "You must not knowingly leave the federal judicial district where you are authorized to reside without first getting permission from the court or the probation officer."

For trips abroad, federal guidance says "Probation officers should seek the express consent of the court before granting a defendant permission to travel outside of the United States." Before asking the court, the officer is supposed to contact the destination country's consulate to check that you can meet its entry rules. If you are approved, you have to check in with your officer when you get back.

Federal parole is stricter on paper. The US Parole Commission requires "specific advance approval" for all foreign travel, and the written request "must demonstrate a substantial need for such travel."

Two more things connect supervision to passports. A probation or parole condition that forbids leaving the US is itself a ground on which the State Department may refuse a passport. And people in prison or on parole for a felony drug conviction involving a border crossing cannot be issued one at all until that period ends.
bullets: These are the federal rules. State probation and parole travel rules vary by state and were not researched for this guide, so ask your own officer how your state handles it.
Leaving without permission can be a violation of your supervision.

sections.heading: Can a Felon Travel to Canada?
paragraphs: Canada is the strictest of the three places in this guide. Canada's immigration department (IRCC) says people who have "committed or been convicted of a crime" may be criminally inadmissible, which means they can be refused entry. Its examples include theft, assault, manslaughter, dangerous driving and "driving while under the influence of drugs or alcohol."

Canada does not look at what your US conviction was called. It matches it to the closest Canadian offence, a process its enforcement manual calls "equivalency," and then applies Canadian penalties. Two levels matter under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA):
bullets: Serious criminality (IRPA 36(1)(b)): a conviction for something that would be punishable in Canada by a maximum of at least 10 years in prison.
Criminality (IRPA 36(2)(b)): a conviction for something that would be an indictable offence in Canada.

An offence that Canada can prosecute either way "is deemed to be an indictable offence, even if it has been prosecuted summarily" (IRPA 36(3)(a)). In practice this means many offences treated as minor in the US can still count.

sections.heading: Can I Go to Canada With a DUI?
paragraphs: A DUI is one of the most common reasons Americans are turned away at the Canadian border. IRCC says "Tougher penalties for impaired driving came into effect on December 18, 2018," and a conviction can now make a person "inadmissible to Canada for serious criminality, whether the crime happened in Canada or outside Canada." Justice Canada lists a maximum of 10 years in prison for alcohol- and drug-impaired driving, first through third offence.

The date of your offence matters. For an impaired driving offence before December 18, 2018, IRCC judges it "based on the penalties in force at the time." Those older offences may count as criminality rather than serious criminality "unless you received a prison sentence in Canada longer than 6 months."

That difference decides your options. A DUI on or after December 18, 2018 counts as serious criminality, so it cannot be "deemed rehabilitated" by the passage of time. For an older DUI, deemed rehabilitation may be possible "if at least 10 years has passed since you completed your sentence." Either way, IRCC says: "There is no guarantee that you'll be issued a TRP or be authorized to enter Canada."

sections.heading: How Can I Get Into Canada With a Criminal Record?
paragraphs: There are three routes, and which one fits depends on how long ago your sentence ended and how serious Canada considers the offence.

Deemed rehabilitation needs no application. You may be deemed rehabilitated after "10 years for one indictable offence" or "five years for two or more summary convictions," if the offence carries a maximum of "less than 10 years" in Canada. To ask at the border, IRCC's self-check requires one conviction in total, at least 10 years since every part of every sentence was finished (including fees, jail and restitution), an offence Canada does not consider serious, and no serious property damage, physical harm or weapon. Approval "is not guaranteed."

Criminal rehabilitation is an application. You become eligible once at least five years have passed since both the end of your sentence (including probation) and the date of the act. You have to show you are rehabilitated and highly unlikely to reoffend, and processing can take "over a year."

A Temporary Resident Permit (TRP) is for people who are still inadmissible, including those less than five years past their sentence. You need "a compelling reason to enter or stay in Canada temporarily," and it is issued "at the discretion of an officer" when your need to enter outweighs the risk to Canadian society. For some minor offences (for example "minor public mischief or theft") where you "served no jail time," a fee-free permit for one visit may be possible. It is not available for serious criminality, sexual offences, robbery, "fraud of C$5,000," "assault causing bodily harm" or "most offences related to driving while under the influence of alcohol or drugs, including cannabis."

The fees are not consistent across IRCC's own pages. IRCC's fee schedule, read on November 20, 2026, lists a TRP at C$246.25, but IRCC's help centre answer, updated November 3, 2026, still says the permit "has a processing fee of C$200." The fee schedule gives no effective date. An official notice shows the TRP fee rose from C$200 to C$229.77 on December 1, 2023, and a news report (not an official notice) says the current amounts took effect December 1, 2025. Check the amount with IRCC before you pay.

sections.heading: Does an Expunged or Sealed Record Count in Canada?
paragraphs: Possibly, and nothing official says otherwise. IRCC's public page does not mention US expungements or sealed records at all. For a pardon granted in another country, it tells people to check with the visa office serving their region whether it is valid in Canada.

IRCC's enforcement manual (dated 2015) says "The effect of a foreign pardon does not automatically render the person admissible to Canada." Officers look at whether the pardon erases the conviction or "merely recognize[s] that rehabilitation has taken place," and in the second case the person is still inadmissible and is expected to apply for rehabilitation.

The only relief Canadian law clearly names is a Canadian record suspension or an acquittal (IRPA 36(3)(b)). We found no official Canadian page that says how a US state expungement or sealing order is treated. Some immigration lawyers write about a court test for this, but we could not confirm it against IRCC's own text, so we are not relying on it here. If your record was expunged and you plan to go to Canada, asking the Canadian visa office or an immigration lawyer before the trip is the safer path.

sections.heading: Can a Felon Travel to Mexico?
paragraphs: Often, yes, but refusal is possible. Mexico's immigration law (Ley de Migración, Article 43) says authorities "podrán negar" (may refuse) a visa, entry or permission to stay in a short list of cases. The first is when a person's record "en México o en el extranjero" (in Mexico or abroad) puts national or public security at risk. Others include not meeting the law's requirements, giving documents that are not authentic, and being subject to an express prohibition by a competent authority.
The law does not list specific crimes, and the word is "may," not "must." Officers can ask you for any information they need to decide.

A Mexican consulate's guidance for Canadians says entry may be refused to someone convicted of a serious crime, and gives examples such as manslaughter, terrorism, drug-related crimes, rape, human trafficking, extortion and tax fraud. The same page also mentions people "facing criminal proceedings," but that reflects older wording of the law; secondary reports say Mexico's Supreme Court struck that part down, and we could not read the court's own statement to confirm it.

What we could not find: any official source saying Mexico systematically checks US visitors' criminal records, or listing which US convictions lead to refusal. We also could not read the Mexican Embassy's FAQ, Mexico's immigration institute pages on this topic, or the US State Department's Mexico page. So the honest answer is that refusal is possible and up to the officer, not automatic.

sections.heading: Can I Be Refused Re-Entry to the US With a Record?
paragraphs: If you are a US citizen, your record is not a reason to keep you out. The federal rule (8 CFR 235.1(b)) is that a person claiming citizenship has to prove it to the officer, normally with a US passport, and the criminal grounds for refusing entry apply to "aliens," meaning non-citizens. A CBP press release from 2014, now marked as archived, says "a U.S. citizen will never be denied entry into the U.S." We did not find a current CBP policy page that says this in so many words.

Getting back in is not the same as walking free, though. In an April 2025 case, a US citizen crossing at the Hidalgo bridge was sent to secondary inspection, where database checks turned up a felony warrant, and CBP handed him to the county sheriff "to await criminal proceedings." If there is any chance of an open warrant in your name, it is worth clearing it up before you travel.

Non-citizens, including green card holders, are in a different position, because the criminal grounds of inadmissibility can apply to them. That is outside what this guide covers, and an immigration attorney is the right person to ask before any trip.

keys.Can I Get a Passport With a Felony?: No federal statute or regulation we read lists having a criminal record in general as a reason to deny a US passport.
keys.What Can Stop Me Getting a Passport?: The one conviction-based rule that is mandatory is for drug offenses involving a border.
keys.Can I Leave the Country While on Probati: For trips abroad, federal guidance says "Probation officers should seek the express consent of the court before granting a defendant permission to travel outside of the United States."
keys.Can a Felon Travel to Canada?: Canada does not look at what your US conviction was called.
keys.Can I Go to Canada With a DUI?: A DUI on or after December 18, 2018 counts as serious criminality, so it cannot be "deemed rehabilitated" by the passage of time.
keys.How Can I Get Into Canada With a Crimina: The fees are not consistent across IRCC's own pages.
keys.Does an Expunged or Sealed Record Count: We found no official Canadian page that says how a US state expungement or sealing order is treated.
keys.Can a Felon Travel to Mexico?: The law does not list specific crimes, and the word is "may," not "must."

next_steps: Find out whether anything on the passport list applies to you right now: an open warrant, a travel condition in your probation or parole, child support arrears or a federal tax debt. Your probation officer, your state child support agency and the IRS can each tell you where you stand.
If you are under supervision, ask your probation or parole officer in writing about international travel well before you book anything.

Planning on Canada? Work out the date your sentence (including probation and fines) ended and the date of any DUI, then compare them to the deemed rehabilitation, criminal rehabilitation and TRP rules above. Confirm the current fee with IRCC before paying.

Look into clearing your record where you live. Our /states pages cover each state's rules, costs and attorneys, and /free-expungement-help lists free legal aid by state. Keep in mind that a US expungement may not settle things with Canada.
For DUI-specific timelines, see /guides/how-long-does-a-dui-stay-on-your-record, and for felonies, /guides/how-long-does-a-felony-stay-on-your-record.
